To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the time course of the PDE activity in dark-adapted rods is determined by kinetics of two processes that shape the PDE activity wave: rhodopsin shut-off and transducin turnover; (ii) the kinetics of rhodopin shut-off is not under adaptation control, whereas the kinetics of transducin turnover is; and (iii) the kinetics of arrestin binding is adaptation independent and cannot be the sole factor that controls the recovery phase of the PDE

the time course of flash-induced PODE activity in frog rods is shaped by two processes that have characteristic times near ≈0.5 and ≈2 seconds and that are accelerated by light adaptation to the same extent; and that the time constant that characterizes the recovery from saturating flashes (dominant time constant) is not adaptation dependent.
(1) The kinetics of PDE activity in rods is adaptation dependent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the time course of PDE activity and its adaptation.
the kinetics of phototransduction cascade in frog rods.
the kinetics of the key steps that determine the speed and sensitivity in phototransduction cascade.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both rhodopsins and transducins shut-offs are under adaptation control.
the kinetics of rhodogsin and transducine turn-offs are not only key factors in setting speed and sensitivity of phototransduction but also the main targets for light adaptation.

the kinetics of the frog rod PDE activity are shaped by both rhodopsins and transducin, and the adaptation control of both processes is involved in the light-induced changes in the time course of the PDE response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the time course of the PDE activity in dark adapted frog rods is controlled by rhodopsin inactivation and that the effect of light adaptation is due to the acceleration of both rhodopsine and transducin quenching.
light adaptation in frog rods is achieved by a coordinated action of rhodopsins and transducins.

light adaptation is achieved in frog rods by the same two mechanisms as in mammals, i.e. by acceleration of rhodopsine shut-off and transducin turnover, but the relative contribution of the two mechanisms is different.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rhodopsin shut-off in frog rods is a two-stage process that involves phosphorylation followed by arrestin binding.
the time course of the PDE response to a flash can serve as an experimental probe of adaptation-dependent regulation of rhodopsins and transducin.
the kinetics of PDE activity is shaped by at least three processes: rhodopsin inactivation by phosphorylation and arrestin binding, and transducin quenching.
